@NaveenGRao sold Nervana to Intel and MosaicML to Databricks. His third company, @unconvai, is building something that looks nothing like a GPU.

Its US AI investment arm, HYAICO, holds convertible preferred stock equal to 9.1% of Penguin. It paid $377m for a stake SK Telecom bought for $200m in 2024, in a transfer inside SK Group. The logic: Penguin is now mostly a memory business, and it builds and runs the AI clusters that memory goes into. For a memory maker that is a customer, a channel and a window into demand.

The catch: the investor agreement includes a standstill on buying more shares and a requirement to vote with Penguin's board. SK hynix cannot creep to control. A deal would have to be friendly and negotiated.

text:
Some takeaways from this report.

$60B of new AI orders in 13 weeks. $132B backlog. Full year raised by $10B. And every order "rigorously vetted for customer quality and access to capital, land and power." That's Dell directly answering the circular financing fear. Demand strong enough that you can turn away unvetted buyers is not what a bubble top looks like.

Q4 EPS guides down sequentially on rising component costs, and inventory nearly tripled to feed the backlog. Great quarter, tougher margin road ahead.

Bigger picture, Dell is the backbone of this buildout. They assemble the racks, test them, and stand them up. 

The backbone says demand is accelerating across 7,500+ customers, so everything downstream of those racks eventually gets its piece. Connectivity, power, cooling, all of it.

$TSM is my highest-conviction holding into 2027 here's why.

1. I don't have to pick the AI winner.

Nvidia's GPUs and the custom chips from Broadcom, Google and Amazon are mostly built at TSMC. Every debate about GPUs versus custom silicon, or which lab ends up on top, is a debate about TSMC's customers. Share moving between them matters far less to TSMC than the total being spent. High-performance computing is now 68% of revenue.

2. The growth is accelerating at a scale that shouldn't allow it.

Q3 revenue grew 50.9% year on year. October revenue grew 59.7%. Management raised its 2026 growth forecast to about 44% in dollars, from "slightly over 40%" in July. This is a company that will do well over $150bn of revenue this year.

3. The margins tell you about the competition.

Gross margin was 66.4% and operating margin 58.7% last quarter, while absorbing the start-up cost of 2nm and of new fabs in Arizona, Japan and Germany. Press reports point to another round of wafer price increases in 2027, which TSMC has not confirmed. A company that can raise prices on Nvidia and Apple does not have a real competitor at the leading edge.

4. The next leg is already in production.

2nm went from nothing to 8% of wafer revenue in three quarters, and capacity is set to more than double in 2027. New nodes dilute margins first and add to them later. That pattern played out at 5nm and 3nm, and I expect it again.

AMD $AMD just got its first Helios rack running inside a Microsoft Azure lab, and the stock still broke below $400.

AMD says Microsoft accepted delivery this fall, powered up its first Helios rackscale system, and reports it is successfully running early workloads in validation. Azure plans to deploy Helios at scale and is expected to be among the first clouds to put it to work on AI inference. Per Microsoft, each liquid-cooled rack packs 72 MI455X GPUs, 18 EPYC "Venice" CPUs and 31 TB of HBM4.

Why it matters: Helios is AMD's answer to Nvidia's rack scale systems, and a hyperscaler running real workloads on it is the proof point the second half ramp needs. But this is a lab, not a customer deployment. No rack counts or financial terms were shared.

The tape did not care. AMD traded as low as $396 Tuesday, its first time under $400 since May and roughly 40% below its $649.42 high on Oct. 6, as the whole AI basket gave back Monday's Nvidia rally. text:
Beyond Warren Buffett buying shares of $TPL as a teenager in the 1940s, Murray Stahl of Horizon Kinetics discovered the company nearly five decades later.

Murray Stahl's first report for his new research service Horizon was about Texas Pacific Land $TPL and over several decades he built a position in the company that made him the largest shareholder. 

We came across Murray and TPL because he or his firm would constantly buy shares on the open market, often times just a few shares a day. 

The P symbols you see on the chart below are some of those purchases. 

I know at least two investment managers who had a chance to work directly with Murray and had nothing but nice things to say about him. 

He passed away earlier this year, the insider purchases stopped a few weeks ago and $3 billion acquisition of EagleRock Land $EROK was announced yesterday.

As I looked at the deal announcement come through, a thought crossed my mind: What would Murray think about this decision?

Hopefully we will explore the answer to that question in our next Merger Arbitrage Mondays article, unless we see a more interesting deal or a pre-deal situation come through by the end of this holiday shortened week.

text:
Meta $META's Muse AI agent can now shop Walmart's Black Friday deals and check out for you, and it is a real test of agents with a spending limit.

Per Walmart's instructions for Muse as reported by The Verge, you tell Muse what you need, sign in to Walmart, and the first time you add an item you set up an Agent Profile with a spending limit. Then you check out inside the Muse conversation with a card saved in your Walmart account, at the same prices as http://Walmart.com. The rollout runs through Walmart's Agent Gateway and its Sparky assistant, and Walmart says Muse is just the start, with other agents on the way.

The guardrails come from Walmart's Oct. 21 announcement, which is confirmed: each agent gets its own profile, customers can require approval on every purchase or allow purchases within a limit such as $50, $100 or $200, and Walmart says agents see the same prices a human would.

Why it matters: Amazon and eBay have blocked AI agents, while Walmart is opening the door on its own terms. For Meta, Muse gets a path from chat to checkout at the biggest retailer in the country right as holiday spending peaks. For the AI compute story, every agent that books, compares and buys is inference demand that never shows up in a clickstream.

Caveat: launch details are as reported. The start date moved between Nov. 23 and Nov. 24 in Walmart's own messages to The Verge, and no usage, revenue share or Meta commentary has been disclosed.

$KSS analyzing with @spotgamma tools 

#retail hot $WMT $DLTR $TJX 

Kohl’s (KSS) is surging +16.6% to $24.73 following a Q3 FY26 earnings beat and raised guidance this morning, putting it just pennies below its $25.00 Call Wall.

$KSS sits right underneath the $25 Call Wall (highlighted in red), which holds the largest concentration of positive call gamma on the board (with top gamma and delta centered in the December 18, 2026 expiration).

Notice the cumulative gamma curve (orange line) and strike bars—KSS sits in a heavily negative net gamma regime (-6.9M Call Gamma / -3.65M Put Gamma), meaning dealers are net short calls across the $20–$25 strikes and must buy shares as price rises to stay delta-hedged. 

Furthermore, with KSS carrying high short interest (~60%+ of float), taking out $25.00 forces both dealer delta-buying and short-covering simultaneously.

Post-Earnings IV Crush & Skew: 1-month implied volatility sits at 80.92% (IV Rank 63.26%) with a $1.08 implied move, and Skew Rank is elevated at 96.00% as traders aggressively bid up upside calls following the beat. 

Once price clears $25.00, the next notable call gamma bars sit at $26, $28, and a larger cluster at $30.

text:
$MSFT 

Analyzing with @spotgamma tools

Watch the HEDGE WALL.

As long as MSFT stays below $497.50, "hedge wall" dealers remain in negative gamma—meaning upside moves can stall as dealers fade rallies toward $497.50–$500, and any drop back under $490 accelerates downside momentum.

A sustained push above $497.50 and $500 flips dealers into net positive gamma. Because the $500 strike holds the tallest call gamma bar on the board, clearing $500 triggers supportive dealer delta-hedging flows toward the $525 Call Wall (with top gamma concentrated in Dec 18, 2026 and top delta in Jan 15, 2027).

zh_summary: $SPCX 下跌 6%，因消息指 $TSLA 和 $SPCX 已任命五位董事商討兩家 Elon Musk 領導公司潛在合併協議的細節。最可能的結構是 SPCX 換 TSLA 的全股票交易，基於今日市值和 TSLA 25% 溢價將需要 SPCX 股份 52% 稀釋。3.6 萬億美元的總規模將使其成為公司史上最大合併。在這些股票換股票交易中，收購方股份通常在完成前下跌。五位董事包括三名來自 $TSLA 和兩名來自 $SPCX。自 SPCX 六月 IPO 於 135 美元以來，$TSLA 下跌 5.6%，$SPCX 下跌 7.7%，而 SPX 下跌 3.4%。
text:
$SPCX -6% on news that $TSLA and $SPCX have named five directors to hash out details of a potential merger agreement between the two Elon Musk-led firms.  As we have discussed before, the most likely structure  is a SPCX-for-TSLA all equity deal, which based on today’s market caps and a 25% premium for TSLA would require 52% dilution in SPCX shares.  The $3.6T total size of this deal would make it the largest merger in corporate history.  As we have warned, in these equity-for-equity deals the acquirer’s shares normally fall pre-close as investors try to lock in proceeds despite a 12-18 month period from deal announcement to deal close. 

The five directors include three from $TSLA and two from $SPCX to ‌guide two special committees handling merger negotiations. The directors are Roelof Botha and Randy Glein from SpaceX ​and Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung ​from Tesla, The Financial Times reported on Tuesday.   $TSLA is -5.6% and $SPCX -7.7% vs SPX -3.4% since SPCX’s June IPO at $135.
